entries.title: US disputes reports of trying conditions on carrier in Gulf
entries.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called reports of poor conditions and mental health strain aboard the USS Abraham Linclon aircrafter carrier in the Middle East "completely misrepresented." Senators want an investigation.
entries.content:
United States of America

US disputes reports of trying conditions on carrier in Gulf

August 13, 2026

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called reports of poor conditions and mental health strain aboard the USS Abraham Linclon aircrafter carrier in the Middle East "completely misrepresented." Senators want an investigation.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which as spent a record-breaking number of days at sea during a period of more than eight months with only brief stops at ports. 

Hegseth called recent reporting in two military-focused outlets in the US, the Navy Times and the Stars and Stripes, "completely misrepresented."

The reports had quoted relatives of sailors recounting stories of poor conditions on board and even a thwarted attempt by a crewmember to throw themselves overboard.

What did Hegseth say about conditions?

The 5,000-person aircraft carrier left San Diego in November for what was scheduled to be a Pacific deployment.

It was subsequently rerouted to the Middle East ready for what the Trump White House called Operation Epic Fury, and has been in the Persian Gulf or the wider region since January amid the war with Iran. 

"We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment," Hegseth told reporters during a visit to Panama on Thursday. "Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it's incredible."

Longer deployments at sea, particularly in wartime with higher stress and danger levels and fewer chances for rest and recreation, have always been a challenge for the US Navy.

Senate calls for inspection visit

A day earlier, Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego said he was calling for an official oversight visit to the USS Abraham Lincoln by a bipartisal Senate Delegation to "investigate the alarming conditions."

"Unlike Donald Trump, I've seen active duty," Gallego said. "They way he's treating our service members as he carries out this illegal war is not just disgusting; it's dangerous. These sailors are owed a sense of when they will go home."

Gallego repeated the call on Thursday, saying Congress "needs to do its job and hold this administration accountable."

Senator Richard Blumenthal also called for the Navy to account for conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, noting "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns" and other problems aboard the Lincoln.

What did the military media outlets report?

The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes have had their eye on the USS Abraham Lincoln's record-setting deployment for months but both revisited the issue in depth this week. This followed a direct appeal late last week by family members to Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao and other senior officials in town hall meetings.

The deployment has included 40 days of continuous combat operations in the US Fifth Fleet area of operations and 250 consecutive days at sea, including a record-breaking number of days without even a port stop, restocking supplies at sea and by air as best as the crew could.

"We already had an instance where watch standres had to stop someone from jumping," Stars and Stripes quoted one sailor as saying.

It also noted various supply and service issues affecting morale, like food rationing, water shortages, and a stretch of more than a week when crew could not do laundry.

It said that many of these issues had since improved, as had mail delivery services — but nevertheless reported a situation of deteriorating morale where, as one sailor put it, "All we want is a date home."

The Lincoln made a brief port call in Oman in early July. Stars and Stripes reported, that allowed it to stock up on valuable producted like fresh fruit and vegetables, but sailors were only permitted to disembark into a secure compound within the port. The ship had also briefly docked in Guam in December, but again with limited shore leave. In the interim it spent the longest period at sea without ever docking in US military histrory.

The Reuters news agency on Thursday cited a US official, who it said was speaking on condition of anonymity, as saying that another aircraft carrier — the USS George Washington — was headed to the region to relieve the Lincoln. The Wall Street Journal in the US carried similar reports on Thursday. The ship departed Vietnam earlier this week.

Hegseth, Trump both indicate much longer deployment conceivable

When asked about what the US calls its "blockade" of Iran's ports — with the Lincoln a crucial command and air-superiority component in the operation — Hegseth said that the US could continue to enforce it for as long as it wished. 

"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," he said.

President Donald Trump had claimed on Wednesday that the navy had "total control" of the Strait of Hormuz and speculated that he might try to permanently police it. 

"The USA has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!" Trump wrote online. "Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' and there is nothing Iran can do about it."

The head of Iran's Basij paramilitary unit, Hossein Taeb, on Thursday disputed Trump's assesment saying the Strait is "under Iran's control and management."

Commercial shipping — whether bound for Iranian ports or for Gulf states, or trying to sail out of the Gulf — has been drastically reduced in volume throughout the conflict, with risks to commercial crews of all stripes from both sides complicating and often halting journeys.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: When the earth moves: six major earthquakes of 2026
entries.summary: Colombia, Venezuela, Mindanao: Thousands have died in powerful earthquakes this year. Six such events show that the magnitude of the quake is not the only factor determining the scale of the disaster.
entries.content:
Colombia

When the earth moves: six major earthquakes of 2026

August 13, 2026

Colombia, Venezuela, Mindanao: Thousands have died in powerful earthquakes this year. Six such events show that the magnitude of the quake is not the only factor determining the scale of the disaster.

Is 2026 a particularly bad year for earthquakes? The number of extremely strong quakes so far this year is not, in fact, unusual. Over the long term, around the world, there are an average of about 15 earthquakes per year registering above magnitude 7 on the Richter scale. By mid-August this year, there had been 10. The devastation some of the quakes have wreaked has, however, been striking.

Venezuela: two quakes in just 39 seconds

On June 24, Venezuela was hit by an earthquake that proved to be by far the deadliest this year. A magnitude 7.2 quake was followed just 39 seconds later by an even stronger one of magnitude 7.5. The north of the country and the capital, Caracas, were the areas worst affected.

According to official figures, more than 6,300 people were killed in the double earthquake. The effects on the impoverished country's infrastructure have also been dramatic. Shortly afterward, a satellite-based assessment by researchers at Oregon State University provisionally concluded that more than 58,000 buildings may have been damaged or destroyed.

Philippines: the strongest quake of the year

With a magnitude of 7.8, the earthquake on June 8 off the southern coast of the Philippine island of Mindanao was the strongest of 2026 so far. It occurred at a depth of about 57 kilometers (35 miles), and was felt across large parts of the island.

At least 107 people were killed. But the fact that, despite the very high magnitude of the quake, far fewer people died in the Philippines than in Venezuela demonstrates that the strength of the quake does not necessarily determine the severity of the consequences.

Colombia: hundreds dead, despite the depth

On August 10, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western Colombia. The epicenter was in the Choco region, near San Jose del Palmar. Although the quake occurred at a depth of 100 kilometers (62 miles), the damage it caused was immense.

More than 250 people are currently estimated to have died. Landslides and damaged roads are hampering the search for victims buried beneath the rubble, as well as the provision of supplies to remote areas. After Venezuela, this quake is the most consequential so far this year for Latin America.

Tonga: powerful earthquake with little damage

On March 24, the earth shook near the island group of Vava'u in the Pacific kingdom of Tonga. With a magnitude of 7.5, it was one of the strongest globally this year. But because there was no severe damage and no deaths, it received almost no attention from the media.

The quake occurred unusually far below the earth's crust, at a depth of around 230 kilometers (143 miles), meaning that the tremors were significantly weakened by the time they reached the surface. To date, there have been no reports of deaths, or damage to infrastructure.

Japan: strong undersea quake off the Sanriku Coast

On April 20, there was an undersea quake off the northeastern coast of Japan. The US Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 7.4.

This region, the Sanriku Coast area in Iwate prefecture, achieved terrible notoriety after the catastrophic earthquake and tsunami there in 2011, which also resulted in the Fukushima nuclear disaster. A tsunami warning was issued after this year's earthquake, too, but fortunately the region was spared the devastation of that magnitude 9 quake 15 years ago.

There was no major tsunami this time, but the quake illustrated once again how much Japan is affected by its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire. This 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) volcanic belt runs around the edge of the Pacific Ocean where several tectonic plates collide.

Afghanistan: weak, but deadly

The earthquake in the northeastern Afghan province of Badakhsham on April 3 only reached a magnitude of 5.8, which puts it right at the bottom of the list of the strongest earthquakes this year. Despite this, at least 12 people were killed, which is why it counts as one of the most significant quakes of 2026.

In poorer countries, even slight tremors can have deadly consequences. The risks are heightened by inadequate building construction, the difficulty of accessing remote areas and underdeveloped disaster response protocols.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Israeli military moves as settlers besiege 3 West Bank homes
entries.summary: Israel's military has moved to try to stop a group of settlers from besieging three homes in the occupied West Bank. One was owned by a Palestinian American, prompting an unusually sharp rebuke from the US ambassador.
entries.content:
Israel

Israeli military moves as settlers besiege 3 West Bank homes

August 13, 2026

Israel's military has moved to try to stop a group of settlers from besieging three homes in the occupied West Bank. One was owned by a Palestinian American, prompting an unusually sharp rebuke from the US ambassador.

Israel has sent soldiers to try to protect three homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra that have been surrounded by a small group of Israeli settlers for several days. 

One of the three homes is owned by a Palestinian American, and the incident prompted an unusually critical reponse from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically considered an ally of Israel's settler movement. 

The case comes amid continued Israeli settlement building, which is considered illegal under international law, in parts of the occupied West Bank, and allegations from critics of the Israeli government that it sometimes turns a blind eye to, or does too little to prevent, settler violence against Palestinians.

What is happening and where?

Starting on Sunday, a group of settlers started gathering around three houses in the village of Qusra.

One of the buildings belongs to Palestinian-American homeowner Loui Ridi. Local officials said the settlers sometimes numbered several dozen. They supposedly threw strones, attempted to bring down a stone wall, and prevented occupants from leaving their homes as their supplies dwindled.

Ridi's brother, Qusai Abu Rida — who had holed up in the house with his son — said on Thursday morning that they had been moved to another home by the Israeli military but still could not leave the area some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Palestinian city of Nablus. Loui Ridi resides in Ohio but owns the property.

Israel's IDF military said its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" near the homes, and detained one Israeli. It wasn't immediately clear if the individual was subject to arrest or investigation, or just detention.

The local mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, said that Israeli forces evacuated seven Palestinian households from their homes to make space for soldiers to take up positions in the village. He said that the settlers remained in other parts of the village, despite being removed from their outposts.

Locals said the village was on effective lockdown.

"No one is allowed to enter. Even food and water are prohibited from reaching those besieged," the Associated Press cited Yasser Ahmad, a resident of a neighboring village, as saying as he watched the operation unfold from one hilltop over.

Qusra is in one of the most violent pockets of the northern West Bank, surrounded by settlements. Its mosque was damaged in attacks last month.

What did US Ambassador Huckabee say about the incident?

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically a supporter of the Israeli settler movement — but also critical of settler violence — spoke out in unusually sharp terms against an incident impacting a US citizen in the West Bank.

"The actions of those doing this to this family's home is criminal," he said. "Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting. No excuse for such thuggish behavior."

However, Huckabee also repeatedly defended both US and Israeli authorities response to the incident, saying the US Embassy in Jerusalem had been "very involved," and that "the IDF and Israel Police have gone at our request to remove the Israeli terrorists doing this."

He later repeated this message, posting video footage seeming to show Israeli security vehicles driving into the area.

The UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory on Thursday called on the Israeli authorities to "immediately" act against the settlers .

"These criminal actions by the settlers, supported or acquiesced to by Israel, the occupying power, are making life unbearable for these Palestinian families, and are clearly aimed at forcing them to leave their homes and land," it said in a statement.

EU foreign policy spokesperson Anitta Hipper called on Israel to take "concrete action to prevent settler violence."

What's the wider issue with West Bank settlement building and settler violence?

Palestinians and some in the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians, as such cases have increased in recent years since the October 7 attacks and amid the war in Gaza.

Israeli government officials tend to describe the violence as the actions of a few fringe youth acting outside the law. The UN's human rights office (OHCHR) said 18 Palestinians have died in the first seven months of this year in attacks involving settlers.

Most of the international community condemns Israeli settlement building in the West Bank as an impediment to a lasting peace and the so-called two-state solution.

More than 500,000 Israelis live — most with but also some without Israeli government authorization and support — in the West Bank, which is home to roughly 3 million Palestinians.

The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 Six-Day War, as part of a future state. Many settlers and some members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government claim the area should belong to Israel, often citing a mixture historical, religious and security reasons.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Ukraine's monthly civilian casualties highest since 2022
entries.summary: UN monitors say civilian casualties in Ukraine hit their highest monthly level since the start of Russia's full-scale war. The latest attacks included a Russian drone strike on a train, killing two workers. DW has more.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine's monthly civilian casualties highest since 2022

Published August 13, 2026last updated August 13, 2026

UN monitors say civilian casualties in Ukraine hit their highest monthly level since the start of Russia's full-scale war. The latest attacks included a Russian drone strike on a train, killing two workers. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • The UN says Ukraine has seen its highest monthly civilian casualty toll since March 2022
  • Ukrainian strikes have hit a major Russian refinery site deep inside the country
  • A Russian military officer was killed in a bombing in Sevastopol, where five people also died during disposal work after a Ukrainian drone attack
  • Ukrainian officials said a Russian drone destroyed a train's engine, killing the driver and his assistant

Here is a roundup of the key developments in Russia's war in Ukraine on Thursday, August 13, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Ukraine reportedly offers Russia halt to Black Sea civilian target attacks

Ukraine reportedly offers Russia halt to Black Sea civilian target attacks

Ukraine has offered Russia a mutual halt to attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea region.

A source told the Reuters news agency Kyiv sent the proposal through a third party and is still waiting for a response from Moscow.

The move comes as both countries accuse each other of increasing strikes on vessels linked to agricultural exports.

Ukraine has relied on alternative shipping routes after Russian strikes near the key grain-export hub of Odesa prompted many shipowners to suspend port calls.

Meanwhile, Russia has halted operations at all three terminals at the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk following a Ukrainian attack, a move expected to further reduce Russian grain exports.

The latest disruptions have raised concerns about global food supplies, while the Kremlin and Russia's Foreign Ministry have not commented on the reported proposal.

Skip next section Russia faces further grain export cuts after port shutdowns

Russia faces further grain export cuts after port shutdowns

Russia is set to cut grain exports further this month after operations were halted at its main Black Sea and Azov Sea ports, with another major terminal suspending activity.

KSK, Russia's largest sea grain terminal, on Thursday said it had stopped operations for safety reasons, meaning all three grain terminals at the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk are now out of action.

Two other Novorossiysk terminals, NZT and NKHP, were shut on Wednesday following a large Ukrainian drone attack on the port.

Sources told Reuters that NKHP's loading gallery suffered severe damage and could remain offline for months, while NZT sustained lighter damage and may reopen sooner.

Andrey Sizov, head of the Sovecon consultancy, said the shutdowns could reduce Russian grain exports by between 700,000 and 1.2 million tonnes in August alone.

He warned that markets were underestimating the risk posed by the growing escalation in the Black Sea and Azov Sea region.

Skip next section Poland arrests Russian over alleged assassination plot

Poland arrests Russian over alleged assassination plot

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk says a Russian national has been detained on suspicion of planning to kill a Ukrainian-American dual citizen in Warsaw on Moscow's orders.

Tusk said Polish security agents and police arrested the suspect on August 7 with help from US authorities, preventing what he described as a planned "execution."

Tusk did not publicly identify the intended victim but said the person was considered "inconvenient" by the Kremlin.

He described the case as the first known instance in which someone allegedly acting on Russian orders had prepared an attack against a US citizen on the territory of another NATO member. Tusk warned that Poland should expect further attempts to target people viewed as threats by the Kremlin.

Poland has repeatedly accused Russia of sabotage and other covert operations since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

In June, Russian caricaturist and Kremlin critic Semyon Skrepetsky, whose real name was Robert Kuzovkov, was shot dead in eastern Poland. Tusk later described the killing as a "political murder."

Russian government opponents have also previously been targeted in attacks elsewhere in Europe, including in the UK, Germany and Lithuania.

Skip next section Russian strike hits Ukraine's largest Danube grain port

Russian strike hits Ukraine's largest Danube grain port

Russia has struck Ukraine's largest grain export port on the Danube, damaging infrastructure and causing a fire, Ukrainian authorities said.

The overnight attack hit the port of Izmail in the southern Odesa region near the Romanian border and also knocked out power in southeastern parts of the city.

Local authorities said port infrastructure was damaged in the attack, though they did not immediately give details of the extent of the destruction.

Izmail is a major hub for Ukrainian exports of grain and other commodities, particularly when access to Black Sea ports is disrupted.

Romania, a NATO and European Union member, scrambled two fighter jets after what its Defence Ministry described as an "aerial target" briefly entered Romanian airspace.

The ministry said the object remained in Romanian airspace for around two minutes before heading back toward Ukraine, where explosions were later heard.

Record-low water levels on the Danube could further complicate efforts to move grain through the river.

Skip next section Ukrainian drones strike major Russian oil refinery

Ukrainian drones strike major Russian oil refinery

Ukrainian drones struck one of Russia's largest oil-refining complexes deep inside the country, according to Ukraine's military, marking the fourth such attack in three days.

Ukraine's General Staff said the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat refinery and petrochemical complex in Russia's republic of Bashkortostan was hit overnight, sparking a fire.

The facility is about 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from the Ukrainian border, southeast of Moscow.

Ukraine's military described it as one of Russia's largest oil-refining and petrochemical complexes.

The plant can process up to 74 million barrels of oil a year and produces gasoline, diesel and other petroleum products.

Kyiv has intensified attacks on Russia's energy sector in recent months, arguing that oil revenues help finance Moscow's war effort.

Skip next section Ukrainian strike shuts major Russian refinery for months

Ukrainian strike shuts major Russian refinery for months

Separately, a Ukrainian long-range strike has forced a major Russian oil refinery hit earlier this week to shut down completely, with repairs expected to take up to six months, according to a regional official.

The attack on the Orsk refinery took place around 1,300 kilometers (810 miles) from the front line.

Orenburg regional Governor Yevgeny Solntsev said the plant had been taken entirely out of operation.

"The equipment is imported, and given sanctions, repairs will take up to six months," he wrote on social media.

"The plant has been completely shut down," Solntsev added, saying authorities were "preparing for the worst-case scenario."

The region may now need to bring in fuel from elsewhere to cover any shortages.

The closure could add fresh pressure to Russia's fuel market, where shortages and rising prices have already affected drivers and businesses in recent months.

Many Russian regions have at some point introduced limits on commercial fuel sales, including caps on purchases and other forms of rationing.

Skip next section Five killed defusing explosive device in Crimea

Five killed defusing explosive device in Crimea

In separate news from the bombing that killed a Russian naval officer in Sevastopol, Crimea's Moscow-appointed figurehead said five people were killed while trying to defuse an explosive device in the same city.

Mikhail Razvozhayev said four emergency-service bomb disposal specialists and a security guard were carrying out clearance work following a Ukrainian drone attack. He said all five people involved were killed.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defences shot down or intercepted 362 Ukrainian drones overnight across several Russian and Russian-controlled regions, including Crimea.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up long-range aerial attacks as the war enters its fifth year.

Skip next section Russian military officer killed in Crimea bomb attack

Russian military officer killed in Crimea bomb attack

A Russian military officer was killed in a bomb attack in Russian-annexed Crimea, with authorities saying a woman was arrested on suspicion of carrying out the killing for Ukrainian special services.

The attack happened on Thursday in Sevastopol, Crimea's largest city, the region's appointed head, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said. Ukraine did not immediately comment.

Russian Telegram channels reported that the victim was Robert Shageyev, a former Ukrainian naval officer who switched allegiance to Russia when Moscow annexed Crimea in 2014.

The channels said Shageyev had been commanding the Ukrainian submarine Zaporizhzhia at the time.

Razvozhayev did not officially name either the victim or the suspect.

Russia's FSB security service said the woman detained in connection with the killing was a Russian citizen, according to state news agency TASS.

Authorities suspect her of acting on behalf of Ukrainian special services.

An unofficial Ukrainian website, Myrotvorets, which lists people it regards as war criminals or traitors, said Shageyev had been "liquidated."

Skip next section Putin visits disputed Kuril Islands amid Ukraine tensions

Putin visits disputed Kuril Islands amid Ukraine tensions

Russian President Vladimir Putin has visited the disputed Kuril Islands for the first time, drawing a strong protest from Japan.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the trip would further strain already difficult relations with Moscow over Russia's war in Ukraine.

Read more about the story here.  

Skip next section Ukraine civilian casualties hit highest level since 2022

Ukraine civilian casualties hit highest level since 2022

Civilian casualties in Ukraine have climbed to their highest monthly level since the early weeks of Russia's full-scale invasion, according to the United Nations.

The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said it verified at least 437 civilians killed and 2,610 injured in July, a 30% rise from June and 70% more than in July 2025.

July recorded the highest overall number of civilian casualties since March 2022, while the number of people killed was the highest since May 2022.

The UN said the true toll was likely higher, with some reports still being verified.

Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, the UN has verified at least 16,874 civilian deaths and 51,273 injuries in Ukraine.

Long-range missiles and drones remained the biggest cause of civilian casualties in July, accounting for 38% of the total. Short-range drones operating close to the frontline accounted for another 27% of casualties.

“Civilians are facing intensified risks from the increased use of missiles and drones in urban centers, glide bombs in cities closer to the frontline, and short-range drones," said head of the mission Danielle Bell.

Russia launched at least 429 missiles during the month, more than twice the number fired in June, according to the UN.

The deadliest attack came on July 2, when Russian forces launched 74 missiles and almost 500 long-range drones, mostly against Kyiv. At least 30 civilians were killed and 104 injured.

Skip next section Russian drone strike on Ukraine train kills two

Russian drone strike on Ukraine train kills two

A Russian drone strike has hit a passenger train carrying hundreds of people in Ukraine's southern Odesa region, killing two railway workers, Ukrainian officials said.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 340 people were on board when a drone struck and destroyed the locomotive.

Zelenskyy said the locomotive driver and his assistant were killed in the attack.

None of the passengers was injured, according to the head of Ukraine's state railway operator.

Footage released by emergency services showed flames engulfing the damaged front of the train.

Zelenskyy accused the drone operator of knowingly targeting a civilian train, saying it would have been impossible not to recognize the nature of the target.

Russian forces have repeatedly struck Ukraine's railway network during the war, hitting trains, stations and other infrastructure.

Kyiv says the attacks are intended both to disrupt transport and logistics and to target civilian life.

Zelenskyy said Russian forces had also launched more than 130 attack drones overnight, with strikes reported across 11 regions.

He again called for additional air defenses and stronger international pressure on Moscow.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The United Nations says civilian casualties in July reached their highest monthly level since the early weeks of the full-scale invasion.

A Russian drone strike has hit a passenger train in Ukraine's southern Odesa region, killing two railway workers but leaving hundreds of passengers unhurt.

The attack came during another heavy night of Russian drone strikes across Ukraine, with Zelenskyy again urging allies to provide more air defenses.

Stay with us for the latest on these stories and other developments in Russia's war in Ukraine.

entries.title: How Germany's drone defense fails
entries.summary: Drone defense is a priority for the German government. The latest dramatic incident involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport shows there are still substantial shortcomings.
entries.content:
Germany

How Germany's drone defense fails

August 13, 2026

Drone defense is a priority for the German government. The latest dramatic incident involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport shows there are still substantial shortcomings.

How could a drone laden with explosives fly unhindered into Leipzig/Halle airport, where it remained apparently unnoticed for several hours? After last week's incident, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."

Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because the drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.

The fact that the drone was loaded with explosives and able to reach the airport demonstrates a new level of threat. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.

Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, warned security expert Nico Lange.

"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.

The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.

The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.

Coordinated response difficult for state, federal police

Germany has so far done little to address the issue of drone defense. Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.

In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.

Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.

Unclear responsibilities

Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.

Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.

Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.

Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?

As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.

A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.

In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."

Airports, train stations still lack protection

There is also lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.

"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."

The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.

The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Eritrea: a rising power along a global shipping artery
entries.summary: Amid growing tensions and security risks in the Horn of Africa, Eritrea, with its strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, is emerging as an important player in the region.
entries.content:
Eritrea

Eritrea: a rising power along a global shipping artery

August 13, 2026

Amid growing tensions and security risks in the Horn of Africa, Eritrea, with its strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, is emerging as an important player in the region.

Across the Horn of Africa, geopolitical interests of various countries continue to cause tensions and conflict as part of the growing competition for political influence over the region.

In its own right, the small country of Eritrea appears to be gaining in importance within this context: The autocratic state run by long-standing ruler Isaias Afwerki controls strategically important coastal points on the Red Sea, especially with its ports of Assab and Massawa.

In July, a series of diplomatic consultations in Cairo involving regional powers like Egypt, Somalia, Eritrea, and a high-ranking US envoy highlighted Eritrea's growing role in helping to coordinate approaches to resolving serious security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea, and to facilitate trade.

Eritrea's unique location along this maritime route is notably becoming more and more strategic in light of international trade conflicts. The small nation's coastline near the Bab-al-Mandab Strait stretches for more than 1,000 kilometers (621.4 miles), bordering Sudan to the northwest and Djibouti to the southeast.

But Eritrea's main strategic importance relies on who is on the other side of the strait, which at its narrowest point measures less than 30 kilometers.

A small country at a strategically important location

"Yemen lies on the other side of the Red Sea, which makes Eritrea's location particularly interesting, as Yemen is in a state of crisis and maritime security in the region is at risk," Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration (CRI) in London, told DW.

"The only safe route in this area runs through Eritrea, where there are currently no security concerns."

The Houthi militia, propped up by Iran, have been attacking merchant ships in the Red Sea from the Yemeni coastline.

For the past ten years, Yemen has also been witnessing one of the world's worst humanitarian crises in its midst: Ongoing violence, economic collapse, droughts and floods have exacerbated the suffering in the country, according to a report published by the UN Refugee Agency last month.

Sayed meanwhile emphasizes that in Eritrea, the strong dictatorship entrenched for decades does not tolerate any type of dissent. In many international freedom indexes, the African nation often only comes second to North Korea.

Since the country was officially founded 32 years ago, there have been no elections in the one-party state under long-time ruler Afwerki.

A unique sense of stability — for now

But this is also exactly why there are no violent conflicts in the country. Compared to other players in the broader region like Ethiopia, Sudan, and Yemen, Eritrea appears to be an island of peace where it is easy to do business.

"For this reason, all countries — including regional powers such as Saudi Arabia and Egypt, which controls the Suez Canal — want to maintain stable relations with Eritrea," Sayed highlights.

At the same time, this could eventually prove to be the country's Achilles' heel: "The country is ruled by a single man, and there are no constitutional institutions. That makes the state very vulnerable should this strongman be removed from power," says Sayed.

There is no strong figure in the 80-year-old autocrat's inner circle seen as a clear successor. This has raised some concern that the security situation could collapse once the president might no longer be in power, according to Sayed.

Alternative to the Strait of Hormuz

Still, Eritrea continues to exert its influence as the Red Sea has emerged a crucial sea route for the world, and especially for the Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, according to Sayed.

The war with Iran has further reinforced the nation's position, as this crisis has once again shown the central geopolitical importance of maritime chokepoints such as Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb.

A viable alternative, should the Strait of Hormuz remain repeatedly blocked, would be for these Gulf nations and their partners to find routes via Saudi ports located further up on the Red Sea.

While the Saudis have pipelines running from some of the interior regions of the country from where oil is extracted and produced to the port of Yanbu-Al-Bahr on the Red Sea, this alternative route could easily be compromised when it comes to security, potentially driving up oil prices even higher than what they currently are.

"For this reason, Eritrea today is of great strategic importance. This has been the case for centuries and will continue to be the case," Sayed emphasizes.

Ethiopia demands direct Red Sea access

Meanwhile, Eritrea's neighbors, particularly landlocked Ethiopia, are fighting hard to maintain access to the Red Sea as a trade route, Sayed adds, in particular for oil exports from the Horn of Africa to the rest of the world, especially to Europe and the Americas.

For decades, Djibouti has dominated regional trade logistics as Ethiopia's most important seaport partner, while Eritrea has been sidelined economically.

But Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has for years been demanding sovereign access to the sea — more than three decades after the country's split with Eritrea: when Eritrea gained its independence in 1993, Ethiopia lost its direct access, and has since been relying on its neighbors for all its sea trade.

However, maintaining a sense of neutrality and balance is proving to be a walk on a tightrope: Earlier in 2026, the fragile relations with between Ethiopia and Eritrea's Asmara region had already threatened to escalate amid a dispute over Ethiopia's access to the maritime trade route.

"The key context for Eritrea's recent strategic maneuvers in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea is the escalating tensions with Ethiopia," says Michael Woldemariam, a researcher at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland and the Atlantic Council.

"Asmara is seeking to forge partnerships that can serve as a counterweight to Addis Ababa. Its recent diplomatic outreach to Egypt, Somalia, the United Arab Emirates' armed forces, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopian opposition groups, and even the US should be viewed against this backdrop," he tells DW.

Meanwhile, a new trade corridor on the Red Sea is also taking shape: In May 2026, Eritrea and Egypt signed an agreement to establish direct freight connections between Egyptian and Eritrean ports on the Red Sea to expand independent trade and supply chains in the region.

A grave record of human rights violations

Still, there are no long-term guarantees with Eritrea, since the country's short history is almost entirely marked by violence, resulting in many people seeking a better life elsewhere.

"The first people fled Eritrea for Sudan in 1967 to escape [former Ethiopian ruler] Haile Selassie's imperial army. In the 1980s, people fled in large numbers from the Ethiopian military dictatorship. Since 2001, people have once again been fleeing in large numbers from human rights violations, military service, war, and a lack of prospects," says Magnus Treiber, a migration researcher specializing in the Horn of Africa at the Institute of Ethnology at the University of Munich.

"The causes of flight have hardly changed. However, since the European Union now offers virtually no opportunities to seek asylum, Eritreans are now fleeing all over the world."

At least 700,000 people have left the country since its founding, which is about a fifth of its total population. The country's population growth, meanwhile, is under 2% — a low number compared to many countries in the region.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: What would a North Korean troop surge mean for Ukraine war?
entries.summary: Ukraine is claiming that North Korea is preparing to send tens of thousands more troops to Russia, where they'll gain valuable battlefield experience.
entries.content:
North Korea

What would a North Korean troop surge mean for Ukraine war?

August 13, 2026

Ukraine is claiming that North Korea is preparing to send tens of thousands more troops to Russia, where they'll gain valuable battlefield experience.

North Korea is preparing a massive troop surge to help its ally Moscow in its war on Ukraine, with up to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed in Russia, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

In late July, the Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops, before adding this weekend that Pyongyang decided to have between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans deployed on Russian territory. He did not specify if this number included the North Korean troops already taking part in the conflict.

In the comments published this weekend, Zelenskyy also warned North Korea was gaining valuable experience in modern warfare and urged South Korea to boost cooperation with Ukraine on air defense and drones. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia.

North Korea has suffered thousands of casualties in the Ukraine war

Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later. Analysts believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region.

Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded.

On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front.

Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality'

South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-weon told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer.

Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country.

"I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW.

Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment.

"Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military."

Will North Koreans watch Russians' back?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, also seemed to signal caution.

"Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW.

"North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han.

"Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to front-line combat in Ukraine."

Russian officials praise North Koreans

"North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said.

The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean casualties, some 2,000 may have been killed.

"Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment," Han said.

"North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery."

North Korean women also moving to Russia

Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops."

"North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979.

"If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added.

"North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel."

Ukraine war used as training ground for North Korean military

According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military."

"However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn.

"A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden."

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Germany: Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive
entries.summary: Rail traffic was suspended in a region of Bavaria and authorities evacuated buildings around a train station after a suspicious object was found on the tracks. Police later confirmed it did not contain explosives.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive

August 13, 2026

Rail traffic was suspended in a region of Bavaria and authorities evacuated buildings around a train station after a suspicious object was found on the tracks. Police later confirmed it did not contain explosives.

Buildings near a train station in the southern state of Bavaria were evacuated as a precaution on Thursday after police said that an object found on the tracks could contain explosives.

Investigators later determined that the object was not an explosive, although criminal police were continuing work at the scene.

A technician had discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen.

Specialists X-rayed the object, which was also lifted using a robot to allow further investigations.

Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged.

Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes.

Edited by: Rob Turner

Germany

Germany news: Far-right leader backs left-wing populist

Published August 13, 2026last updated August 13, 2026

The leader of the far-right AfD in Thuringia, Björn Höcke, has offered to back populist Sahra Wagenknecht as state premier. And heat-related deaths this year are now numbered at some 12,500. DW has more.

Skip next section WATCH: Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships

WATCH: Rhine River drops to record low levels, grounding ships

This summer's heat waves and lack of rain have led to a sharp drop in the levels of Germany's inland waterways. The Rhine River's water levels have sunk to record lows. That's taking a heavy toll on commercial shipping.

Skip next section Porsche reportedly plans to end Taycan production by 2030

Porsche reportedly plans to end Taycan production by 2030

German luxury and sports-car maker Porsche is reportedly planning to stop producing its electric Taycan by 2030 after weak sales left output at its main Stuttgart plant running well below capacity.

German business magazine "Wirtschaftswoche" says Porsche's management and works council had reached an agreement in principle, although it had not yet been put in writing.

The Taycan was Porsche's first fully electric model and initially became the company's flagship EV after production began in 2019. Its second electric model, the Macan SUV, followed in 2024.

Taycan sales have fallen sharply in recent years, however, leaving production at Porsche's Stuttgart headquarters underused.

According to the magazine, Porsche had given up on moving Taycan production to its Leipzig plant or ending the model sooner. The current plan would instead keep production in Stuttgart until 2030.

Porsche had set itself the goal in 2022 of increasing the share of fully electric vehicles to 80% of sales by 2030.

But Porsche has since adjusted its strategy as demand for electric cars has developed more slowly than expected. The Macan is also due to become available again with a combustion engine.

Skip next section Pay for Germany's top executives rises again

Pay for Germany's top executives rises again

Executives at Germany's 40 largest listed companies have seen their average pay rise again, with a typical DAX board member earning more than €3.9 million ($4.5 million) in 2025.

The annual analysis by the shareholder association DSW and the Technical University of Munich found executive compensation increased by 4% compared with the previous year, with a large share coming from performance-related bonuses.

Across all DAX companies, board members earned on average 42 times as much as ordinary employees at their firms.

The widest gap was at Adidas, where executive board members received 106 times the average employee compensation.

The ratio was 75 to one at Volkswagen and 70 to one at healthcare group Fresenius.

Chief executives of DAX companies received an average of around €6.14 million in 2025.

SAP chief Christian Klein topped the ranking with total compensation of about €10.9 million, around 86% of it variable.

Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing received €10.5 million, with around 64% made up of short- and long-term bonuses linked to business performance.

DSW managing director Marc Tüngler said the €10 million mark had been exceeded in two cases, describing it as a level that remained socially and internally sensitive.

German CEO pay remains well below levels at many major companies abroad.

CEOs of non-German companies in the Euro Stoxx 50 received an average of €9.5 million in 2025, while the average among the 30 companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average was €30.5 million.

Skip next section German officials warn against nostalgia for East Germany

German officials warn against nostalgia for East Germany

German officials have warned against romanticizing communist East Germany, saying nostalgia for the former dictatorship risks obscuring its repression and lack of basic freedoms.

The comments came on the 65th anniversary of the construction of the Berlin Wall and just weeks before important state elections in eastern Germany.

Culture Minister Wolfram Weimer said both left-wing and right-wing extremists were trying to play down the crimes of the former East German regime.

He described East Germany as a "brutal dictatorship" without free elections, press freedom or freedom of movement, and pointed to the role of the Stasi secret police, political repression and the fortified border around West Berlin.

Evelyn Zupke, Germany's federal commissioner for victims of the communist dictatorship, also warned against what is commonly known as "Ostalgie" — nostalgia for life in the former East Germany.

"East Germany seems more appealing to some people the further it recedes in history," she told the Rheinische Post newspaper, warning that a nostalgic view could blur the reality of the dictatorship.

Skip next section Day 3 of 4 in Nathalie Pohl's world record Frankfurt-Cologne extreme swim challenge

Day 3 of 4 in Nathalie Pohl's world record Frankfurt-Cologne extreme swim challenge

Extreme swimmer Nathalie Pohl is continuing her swim up the Rhine River (yes, it is still deep enough for this purpose at least!) towards Cologne.

She trying to set a new world record by covering a 200 kilometer stretch from Frankfurt to Cologne in just four days, raising money for charity en route.

Pohl entered the water in Lahnstein, near Koblenz, shortly before 11 a.m. on Thursday. The day's stretch covers some 58 kilometers, ending in Bad Honnef — a short southerly swim upstream from DW's offices on the Rhine in Bonn.

Wednesday's stretch already took her through some of the shallowest segments of the Rhine amid this summer's drought, particularly the bottleneck at Kaub.

Pohl is raising money to improve awareness on the importance of safe swimming among children, and to fund swimming projects and teaching. Her team says they have raised around €85,000 (almost $100,000) so far.

Skip next section Steel giant Thyssenkrupp plows on with Duisburg production, for now, despite Rhine river issues

Steel giant Thyssenkrupp plows on with Duisburg production, for now, despite Rhine river issues

German steel giant Thyssenkrupp says the low Rhine River levels have not yet impacted production at its major facility in Duisburg.

Chief Financial Officer Axel Hamann said that supplies to customers were not presently at risk, as he presented nine-monthly performance figures to the press.

For the moment, he said, the facility was still receiving some deliveries of raw materials — particularly coal for the furnaces — via partially-laden barges on the Rhine.

"If the situation really deteriorates and the ship journeys are stopped altogether, then we could not rule out an effect on results," he said, meaning sales volumes and output.

"We of course do have a few options to adapt the production and the deliveries to our facilities somewhat, so we can continue to work longer with the supplies that we have," Hamann said. He said there were shipping alternatives and that the company was trying to secure more supplies via rail in particular.

"We're still a long way away from letting some of our furnaces run cold," Hamann said.

The company was also looking into potential transport by road networks, he said — but typically coal is seen as a very bulky, heavy and cost-inefficient product to transport using trucks in large quantities. Earlier in the week, a company spokeswoman had suggested that truck transportation was not a realistic option.

Skip next section Drought causing significant crop losses

Drought causing significant crop losses

The lack of rainfall affecting large parts of Germany has severely impacted this summer's harvest, according to an association representing farming companies.

Around 3 million metric tons (3.31 million US tons) of grain and rapeseed have been lost since mid-June, meaning revenue shortfalls of €600 million ($692 million), the German Raiffeisen Association said.

According to the association's expert for cereal markets, Guido Seedler, "that amounts to economic damage of €10 million each dav during the around 60-day hot-weather period from June till the end of the harvest."

The association estimates that this year's grain harvest will be 40.6 million tons, down from 45 million tons in 2025.

"Only the favorable spring weather prevented greater damage," Seedler said, adding that the harvest was still adequate overall but below average.

The German Raiffeisen Association represents 1,600 cooperative companies in agricultural trade and processing.

Skip next section Top executives earning 42 times as much as average workers — study

Top executives earning 42 times as much as average workers — study

Managers at Germany's top listed companies were paid an average of just over €3.9 million ($4.5 million) in 2025, a study has shown.

That means that executives at the 40 companies in the DAX stock index brought home 42 times the pay of an average employee.

The chief executives of DAX companies received pay of an average €6.14 million in 2025, the study by the German shareholder protection association DSW and the Technical University of Munich.

Pay for two chief executives exceeded €10 million: Christian Klein, chief executive of software company SAP, received around €10.9 million, and Deutsche Bank boss Christian Sewing received €10.5 million.

In Klein's case, almost 86% of that came from variable compensation, while 64% of Sewing's pay was made up of short and long-term bonuses linked to business performance.

As high as these sums may seem to many normal citizens, they are relatively modest in international comparison.

Top executives of companies in the Euro Stoxx 50, excluding German ones, received an average of €9.5 million for the 2025 financial year, the analysis showed.

And for chief executives of the 30 companies in the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the average was €30.5 million.

Skip next section UPDATE — Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive on rail track

UPDATE — Buildings evacuated over suspected explosive on rail track

Authorities have begun evacuating buildings around a Bavarian train station as specialists examine a suspicious object on the tracks.

Rail traffic is currently suspended in the area as experts check to see if explosives are present.

Read more about the full story on the suspected explosive in Bavaria here

Skip next section WATCH — A virtual tour of Germany's inner border and the Berlin Wall

WATCH — A virtual tour of Germany's inner border and the Berlin Wall

For 28 years, a nearly insurmountable barrier kept people from fleeing East Germany. Today, it is difficult to imagine what was bitter reality just a few decades ago. A computer animation reveals the vast security system of Germany's inner border and the Berlin Wall, both of which were recreated virtually in the greatest detail.

Skip next section Merz calls for defense of democracy on Berlin Wall anniversary

Merz calls for defense of democracy on Berlin Wall anniversary

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has called on people to keep up the fight to retain freedom and democracy as Germany marks the 65th anniversary of the construction of the Berlin Wall.

"Sixty-five years ago, the leadership of former East Germany had the Wall built. Today, our country has been united longer than it was divided and we live in freedom and peace," Merz wrote on the platform X.

"The lesson of the Wall remains: Freedom and democracy are not a given. We must always fight for them," he wrote.

Merz's remarks come amid a surge in popularity of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party seen by many as anti-democratic in its ideology. 

On August 13, 1961, on what would become known as Barbed Wire Sunday, communist East Germany sealed the border between Berlin’s eastern and western sectors before building a wall that was to divide the city for the next 28 years.

People trying to cross the Wall to leave the authoritarian state were often shot dead, and the barrier came to symbolize the repressive political system behind it.

In remarks to the daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, he commissioner for culture, Wolfram Weimer, warned against "positive distortions of former East Germany" by the far-right AfD and the Left Party.

Weimer criticized such "collective forgetting, repression and downplaying of former East Germany" as the biggest challenge to properly commemorating the crimes of the regime there.

Skip next section Suspicious object halts trains at Bavaria station

Suspicious object halts trains at Bavaria station

Rail traffic through the southern German town of Treuchtlingen has been suspended after police found a suspicious object on the tracks that may contain explosives.

Police in Bavaria's Middle Franconia region said specialist Federal Police units were examining the object, which was discovered in the track bed at Treuchtlingen station.

Police described the item as posing a possible explosive hazard and said specialist officers were carrying out further checks.

The object was being X-rayed late Thursday morning as authorities worked to determine exactly what it was.

Police have also urged people to avoid the area.

Treuchtlingen, a town of around 13,000 people about 150 kilometers (95 miles) north of Munich, is an important railway junction in Bavaria. Regional and long-distance services running through the station connect destinations including Munich and Nuremberg.

Skip next section Heat-related deaths on the rise — Robert Koch Insitute

Heat-related deaths on the rise — Robert Koch Insitute

Several spates of hot weather across Germany this year have caused an estimated 12,500 premature deaths so far, public health authorities have said.

The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) said its figure, released on Thursday, is a conservative estimate.

The worst-affected states were the western states of Saarland and Rhineland-Palatinate, which had more than double the national average of heat-related deaths.

The most deaths were recorded in the age group 85 years or older, at around 6,300. More than 3,100 of those who died were aged between 75 and 84, and nearly 1,900 between 65 and 74.

The severe heat wave at the end of June was especially deadly, with the RKI expecting that around 9,600 people died as a result of heat in the week from June 22 to 28 alone. 

Climate scientists say that heat waves will increase in severity and frequency as the Earth continues to warm, largely owing to the human use of fossil fuels.

Skip next section AfD firebrand Höcke offers to back Wagenknecht as Thuringia state premier

AfD firebrand Höcke offers to back Wagenknecht as Thuringia state premier

The leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the eastern state of Thuringia, Björn Höcke, has offered to back left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht as state premier.

"I am extending my hand to you," Höcke said on Wednesday in a video posted on X.

He urged Wagenknecht to become state premier before a regional election in neighboring Saxony-Anhalt on September 6.

Höcke's offer comes as Thuringia's Premier Mario Voigt of the Christian Democrats (CDU) continues to face pressure after his doctorate was withdrawn over plagiarism claims.

The AfD has said it plans to launch another constructive vote of no confidence against Voigt.

Under Thuringia's constitution, a premier can only be removed if parliament simultaneously elects a successor by a majority. The AfD and BSW together hold the necessary majority, with 47 of the state parliament's 88 seats.

Wagenknecht, has indicated that her party, the anti-migrant, left-wing populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), could abstain in a decisive vote for state premier in Saxony-Anhalt, potentially helping an AfD candidate take office.

The BSW is currently part of Thuringia's governing coalition along with the conservative CDU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

Höcke's AfD is the largest group in the Thuringian state parliament but does not form part of the government.

The move proposed by Höcke would call into question the current consensus among mainstream parties that there should be no cooperation with the far right, known as the "firewall."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

The DW newsroom in Bonn wishes all its readers herzlich willkommen!

You join our coverage of all things Germany as far-right leader Björn Höcke makes what seems at first glance to be an unlikely offer to support a left-wing figure.

Meanwhile, another bout of hot weather is engulfing the country as public health authorities give a frightening toll of heat-related deaths this year.

And Germany is still trying to come up with ways to combat the challenges caused by the much-reduced shipping of cargo on rivers as their waters fall to historically low levels.

Read on here for more on these and other stories.

entries.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi was present as the session marked by a fierce standoff over student protests wrapped up.
entries.content:
India

India news: Parliament ends turbulent monsoon session

Published August 13, 2026last updated August 13, 2026

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was present as the session marked by a fierce standoff over student protests wrapped up.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is closed. It covered the latest developments from India on Thursday, August 13:

  • Both houses of the Indian parliament were adjourned sine die on Thursday
  • A political stalemate between Prime Minsiter Narendra Modi's governement and the opposition showed no signs of abating during the 19-day long proceedings
  • Lawmakers from ruling coalition and the opposition staged demonstrations on the final day of the session, drawing a session overshadowed by protests to close.

Skip next section Tata Trusts begins search for successor to Tata Sons Chairman Chandrasekaran

Tata Trusts begins search for successor to Tata Sons Chairman Chandrasekaran

India's Tata Trusts said it will set up a selection panel to recommend the next chairman of Tata Sons, the holding company of the $180 billion Tata Group.

The decision follows Chairman N Chandrasekaran's announcement that he will not seek reappointment when his term ends in February.

Tata Trusts praised Chandrasekaran's leadership over the past decade and said a committee would be formed as soon as possible.

The conglomerate has faced a year of leadership tensions and boardroom disputes, including concerns about losses at some group companies.

Chandrasekaran said he was stepping down because of a lack of support from one board member. Indian media reports have linked the disagreement to Noel Tata, head of Tata Trusts.

The trusts own 66% of Tata Sons, giving the charitable institutions significant influence over the future direction of India's largest business group.

Karnataka Bandh calls shutdown over Tamil Nadu Cauvery dispute

A statewide shutdown was called in the southern Indian state of Karnataka over the Cauvery river watersharing issue with Tamil Nadu. 

Thursday's agitation came in opposition to the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee directing Karnataka to release 12,000 cusecs of Cauvery river's water to the neighboring state of Tamil Nadu for 15 days.

Protesters have called on the Karnataka government to not release the water saying the state itself is facing water shortages, particularly for drinking and irrigation requirements.

The dispute over sharing the water of the 765-kilometer (475-mile) long river, which resurfaces during rainfall deficit years, dates back a century and has also witnessed bloodshed in the past.

On Thursday, security measures were tightened in several places in the state, including in Mandya, one of the districts associated with the longstanding issue.

According to news agency PTI, the shutdown was met with a mixed response with protests in Mandya and preventive detentions at various locations. However, urban areas like Bengaluru and Mysuru remained unaffected after organizations that had earlier backed the shutdown, pulled away their support.

Protests mark monsoon session of parliament

On the very first day of the monsoon session on July 20, parliament was rocked by a massive youth-led march trying to get to its gates as part of the Cockroach Janta Party movement demanding the resignation of the now former education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities. 

The protesters were met with baton-charges and tear gas firing, and since then the opposition has railed against the violent crackdown, demanding an answer in the parliament from Union Home Minister Amit Shah over alleged police brutality. 

On Wednesday, Shah said that the Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government was ready for a discussion on the student protests which were triggered by a slew of medical entrance exam paper leaks. The leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Congress's Rahul Gandhi, turned down the debate offer saying that the youth wanted answers on who ordered the use of force on protesters and "not a lecture" from Shah.

Addressing a press conference on Thursday, Union Minister of Parliamentarty Affairs Kiren Rijiju accused the opposition of "running away from discussions" and alleged that opposition disruptions affected parliament's productivity.

During the 19-day monsoon session several demonstrations were held by the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties called the INDIA bloc on the parliament premises against the police action and a donation embezzlement controversy linked to the Ram Temple, a shrine central to Modi's Hindu-first politics.

Lawmakers from Modi's ruling coalition also began staging their own demonstrations, including on the last day over another student protest in Jharkhand —  where the Congress party is an ally of the ruling coalition. Tear gas, batons and water cannons were also used to disperse the protesters marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi.
